## The headline result: on the right board, you don't need a sampler at all

I measured this rather than guessed it. **The entire possibility space of an 8×8 board with fleet [4,3,3,2] under the no-touch rule is 3,562,232 configurations, and it fits in 13.6 MB and builds in 68 ms.**

That single fact collapses the whole "hard problem" the brief anticipated. There is no constraint solver, no consistency checker, no propagation engine, no importance sampler, no estimator, no bias. There is a **set of realities**, and every game action is a **filter over that set**. The counter is not estimated — it is `aliveN`, an integer. The ghost fleets are not approximated — they are `alive[rng.int(0, aliveN-1)]`, exactly uniform. The defender is not heuristically evasive — it is provably, exactly, maximally evasive under the greedy criterion.

This is also *exactly* the nostromo-gambit doctrine ("честный отказ лучше подделанного десанта") transposed to the counter: we don't show an estimate dressed as a number.

### Measured universe sizes (all my own runs, exact enumeration or validated SIS)

| board | fleet | no-touch | count | how |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 8×8 | [4,3,3,2] | yes | **3 562 232** | exact, 68 ms |
| 8×8 | [4,3,3,2] | no | 19 999 324 | exact, 396 ms |
| 8×8 | [4,3,3,2,2] | yes | 45 317 068 | exact, 1.5 s |
| 8×8 | [4,3,3,2,2] | no | 783 249 968 | exact, 16.8 s |
| 10×10 | [4,3,3,2] | yes | 7.26×10⁷ | SIS ±0.17% |
| 10×10 | [5,4,3,3,2] | yes | 1.92×10⁹ | SIS ±0.21% |
| 10×10 | [4,3,3,2,2,2,1,1,1,1] (Russian) | yes | **1.869×10¹⁵** | SIS ±2.1% |
| 10×10 | Russian | no | 1.328×10¹⁸ | SIS ±1.0% |

Placement counts: 8×8 → L4:80, L3:96, L2:112, L1:64. 10×10 → L4:140, L3:160, L2:180, L1:100. All < 256, so a placement index is one byte — that's what makes the 4-byte config encoding work.

### RECOMMENDATION: canonical mode is 8×8, fleet [4,3,3,2], no-touch

Not because it's easy, but because it is the largest configuration where the game can be **exactly truthful** for its entire duration, and 3.5 million is a perfect headline number: big enough to feel like a multiverse, small enough that the counter reaches 1 in front of you.

Offer 10×10 Russian as a second mode («БЕЗДНА», 1.87 квадриллиона реальностей) built on Tier 1 below — but ship 8×8 as the default and the tuned experience.

## Tier 0 — the materialised multiverse (canonical mode)

**Representation.** One `Uint8Array(4 × C)`. Config *i* = bytes `[i*4 .. i*4+3]` = placement indices of ship-4, ship-3a, ship-3b, ship-2. Identical ships stored in canonical increasing index order (`3a < 3b`), so the array enumerates *sets*, not sequences — no `/k!` correction anywhere. Cache-friendly, sequential, no pointer chasing, no index array.

**Constraint set = the array itself.** After answer *a* at turn *t*, we compact the array in place, keeping only configs that would have given *a*. Write cursor ≤ read cursor always, so memory never grows and never reallocates. The critical consequence: **the time-indexed "hit but not sunk" constraint needs no bookkeeping at all.** It is enforced automatically because we filtered by the answer computed against the shot-set *as it stood at that moment*. Every constraint the brief worried about — misses empty, hits occupied, killed ship fully within the then-current shots, dead-ship halo empty, each live-hit ship having a surviving unshot cell — is a consequence of having filtered correctly at the time. There is nothing to get wrong later.

**Per-turn work.** Three passes at most:
1. `buildTurnTables(cell)` — 288 bytes of lookup (T4[80], T3[96], T2[112]), values `0` = placement doesn't cover the cell, `1` = covers it and survives the shot, `2` = covers it and dies. Costs 288 iterations. This turns the inner loop from bit arithmetic into **pure array lookups**.
2. `partition` — one linear pass, ≤4 byte loads + ≤4 table lookups per config, incrementing `Int32Array(290)` bucket counters (key 0 = MISS, 1 = HIT, 2+pid = KILL of that specific placement).
3. `compact` — one linear pass keeping the chosen bucket.

The histogram pass (for ghosts + the player's density HUD) is a fourth pass that increments 4 per-placement counters, then expands 288 placement counts into 64 cell counts. Expansion is O(288), not O(C) — a 3× saving over counting cells directly.

### Measured per-turn cost (Node 24, this laptop, single thread)

| turn | alive before | hist ms | partition+compact ms | total |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 3 562 232 | 20.6 | 81.8 | **102.6** |
| 2 | 2 772 244 | 18.7 | 53.1 | 71.9 |
| 5 | 1 174 700 | 9.6 | 25.3 | 35.0 |
| 7 | 578 849 | 2.6 | 10.1 | 12.7 |
| 10 | 183 585 | 0.9 | 3.2 | 4.1 |
| 13 | 45 119 | 0.3 | 0.8 | 1.1 |
| 20+ | < 1000 | ~0 | ~0 | < 0.1 |

Whole game = 360 ms of compute across all turns. Only turns 1–5 are above one frame, and they run in a Worker behind a 400 ms shot animation.

## Tier 1 — sampling (10×10 / bigger fleets)

Exact enumeration on 10×10 Russian is hopeless *for almost the whole game*, and I measured exactly how hopeless: with a 40-million-node budget, a constrained DFS could not complete **until shot 78**, and only got fast (<150 ms) at **shot 84**. So a 10×10 mode is a sampling mode for 80% of its length. Design accordingly and label it honestly in the UI.

Tier 1 = a population of K uniform particles maintained by **Gibbs resampling** (pick a ship, enumerate all its legal placements given the others + the history, choose uniformly — this is exact Gibbs, uniform-stationary), seeded by **SIS restarts**, with the counter driven by a **log-space ratio estimator** anchored on a baked-in constant. Details in `counting`.

Rejected alternatives and why: *rejection sampling* — dies at ~10 constraints, unusable; *DLX/exact cover* — ships aren't an exact cover (empty water is legal), and adapting it buys nothing over the byte-array scan; *DP over columns with a broken profile* — for no-touch battleship the profile state is {empty, terminated, pending-1..3}^10 × 120 fleet-count states ≈ 10⁹, worse than sampling and vastly more code; *per-ship mask intersection with propagation* — gives feasibility, not counts, and counts are the product.

## Three findings that change the game design

**1. The two clocks problem — the multiverse collapses long before the fleet sinks.** Against an optimal player, `N` reaches **1 at shot 31**, but the last ship isn't physically sunk until **shot 62**. Half the game is a mop-up where the player already knows everything. → **Victory condition must be `N == 1`, not "all ships sunk".** Thematically this is the *better* game: you don't sink the fleet, you pin reality until it has nowhere left to be. Then the final cinematic salvo auto-destroys the now-determined fleet. Par ≈ 31, information-theoretic floor = log₂(3 562 232) = **21.76 bits** ⇒ 22 shots. That is a tight, scoreable, replayable 25–35 shot game with a visible perfect score.

**2. The determinism trap.** With a deterministic max-mass defender and no hidden state, *there is no hidden state* — the optimal line is identical every single game. My "split" player scored 31, 31, 31, 31, 31, 31, 31, 31 across eight seeds. Two fixes, both needed: **(a) rift cells** — 2–4 seeded cells no ship may occupy, added to the forbidden mask at build time; the universe is different (and differently sized) every game, so the counter opens on a fresh number like «3 214 118 РЕАЛЬНОСТЕЙ»; **(b) ε-slack answer selection** — among buckets within a factor (1−ε) of the largest, choose by seeded weighted RNG. ε is the difficulty knob and is a direct transposition of nostromo's `slackCp` doctrine (weaken by choosing among near-optimal answers, never by crippling the search).

**3. The all-misses problem.** Under max-mass greedy the defender says MISS almost always — on turn 1 the *densest* cell on the board is occupied in only 22.2% of realities, so the best a shot can do is a 78/22 split = **0.36 bits**. The optimal 31-shot line contains 25 misses, 6 hits and **zero kills before the pin.** A conventional battleship framing would be emotionally flat. → Reframe the feedback: a "miss" is not a miss, it is a **measurement that annihilates 22–43% of all realities**, and the counter + writhing ghost fleet is the payoff. Measured drop-per-shot along the optimal line: −22%, −23%, −26%, −26%, −30%, −30%, −32%, −33%, −36%, −37%, −39%, −43%… an accelerating, always-satisfying curve. Then give the player the **БРАНА-ТОРПЕДА**, which forces the *minimum*-mass answer (guaranteed hit if any reality holds a ship there) as the rare, expensive, spectacular button.

**4. The HUD is the mechanic, not decoration.** A parity hunt/target player (no HUD reasoning) needs **48.3 turns** to pin reality; a density-guided player needs **31**. The ghost fleet and the counter are what make the game the right length. Without them the evasive defender costs a naive player only ~5 shots over a static one — the twist would be invisible. This is the strongest possible argument for the ghost-fleet HUD being load-bearing.

Reference files I worked against: `G:\Другие компьютеры\PAULEKMAN\dev\nostromo-gambit\public\board.js` (the cells-built-once + diffed sprite layer pattern the ghost layer should copy), `G:\Другие компьютеры\PAULEKMAN\dev\nostromo-gambit\src\game\rng.mjs` (drop in unchanged), `G:\Другие компьютеры\PAULEKMAN\dev\nostromo-gambit\public\theme.css`, `G:\Другие компьютеры\PAULEKMAN\dev\nostromo-gambit\src\game\computer.mjs` (difficulty-as-data table to mirror for ε).
data.counting:
## Tier 0: the count is not estimated. It is `aliveN`.

`aliveN` is an `Int32` in the range [1, 3 562 232]. It is the exact number of complete legal fleet placements consistent with the entire answer history. No estimator, no confidence interval, no jitter, no bias, no floating point. The UI prints it with no «≈» and the game may say so out loud, in the house voice:

> «СЧЁТЧИК НЕ ОЦЕНИВАЕТ. ОН ПЕРЕСЧИТЫВАЕТ. КАЖДУЮ.»

Monotonicity is structural, not enforced: `alive_{t+1} ⊆ alive_t` because compaction is a filter over the same array. The counter mathematically cannot go up, cannot jitter, and cannot disagree with the ghost fleet (both read the same array).

Two derived numbers worth showing, both exact and both free:
- **Collapse per shot**: `before − after`, e.g. «СТЁРТО 789 988 РЕАЛЬНОСТЕЙ».
- **Bits**: `log2(before / after)`. The header can carry «ОСТАЛОСЬ 21.76 БИТ» ticking down to 0. This makes the information-theoretic floor (22 shots) legible as a *par*, and it is the single best explanation of why some shots are wasted: a shot at a cell where every reality agrees yields exactly 0.00 bits and the counter does not move.

Rendering rule: below 10 000 print the exact integer with thin-space grouping («8 074»); above that, either the full grouped integer or 3 significant digits + power («3.56 × 10⁶») — but never switch representation mid-fall in a way that looks like a jump. I'd print the full grouped integer always; watching «3 562 232» → «2 772 244» digit-by-digit is the drama.

## Tier 1 (10×10): honest estimation, three layers

**Layer A — the anchor N₀ is a compile-time constant.** For a fixed board+fleet the starting count is a number, not a computation. Bake it in with a comment recording how it was obtained:

```js
// Русский флот 10×10, корабли не касаются. Посчитано SIS-оценкой на 2·10⁶ образцов,
// относительная ошибка 0.7%. Точного перечисления не существует: DFS с бюджетом
// 4·10⁷ узлов не завершается до 78-го выстрела.
const N0 = 1.869e15;
```
(My measured values: Russian no-touch **1.8692×10¹⁵ ±2.12%** at K=200k; touching **1.3283×10¹⁸ ±0.99%**. Ship the number computed at K=2×10⁶ offline for ±0.7%.)

**Layer B — the running counter is a log-space ratio product.** Never estimate the absolute count mid-game; estimate only the *survival fraction* of the chosen answer, which is a ratio of counts from one population and is far lower-variance than an absolute count:

```js
// log-пространство: произведение сорока дробей в обычных числах уползает,
// а сумма логарифмов — нет. И 1.87e15 < 2^53, но 1.33e18 уже нет.
S.logN = Math.log(N0);
// каждый ход:
const f = cnt[chosen] / K;                    // доля популяции, пережившая ответ
S.logN += Math.log(f);
const shown = Math.exp(S.logN);
```
Because the population is uniform (maintained by Gibbs, not by weights), `cnt[chosen]/K` is an unbiased estimator of the true survival fraction, and the ratio form means the K in numerator and denominator largely cancels.

**Layer C — monotone clamp + honest labelling.** `display = min(display_prev, shown)`, floored at 1, printed with a leading «≈». The clamp is justified: the true count is provably non-increasing, so clamping only ever moves the estimate *toward* a value we know is an upper bound. It is a conservative, monotone, non-lying presentation — and the «≈» says exactly what it is.

**Layer D — exact takeover.** Every turn, run the constrained DFS counter with a node budget (I used 4×10⁷; a browser budget of 2×10⁶ nodes ≈ 50 ms is right). If it completes, **drop the «≈» and print the exact integer for the rest of the game.** Measured takeover point on 10×10 Russian with random firing: shot 78 (323 ms at 3.5M nodes), comfortable by shot 84 (51 ms), trivial by shot 90 (1 ms). So the last ~15 shots — the climax — are exactly counted. The moment the «≈» disappears is itself a dramatic beat: «ОЦЕНКА → ПЕРЕСЧЁТ».

**The SIS estimator, named and specified.** Sequential importance sampling with canonical ordering, uniform proposal over the surviving candidate set at each step:

  N̂ = (1/K) Σₖ wₖ,  wₖ = Π_{j=1..m} |C_j^{(k)}|  (wₖ = 0 for dead-end draws, which are *counted in K*)

where `C_j` is the set of legal placements of ship *j* given ships 1..j−1 and the constraint set, and identical ships are restricted to increasing placement index so the sample space is in bijection with *sets* of placements — no `Π kᵢ!` correction. This is Knuth's estimator generalised (Chen–Diaconis–Holmes–Liu sequential Monte Carlo for counting). Variance estimate: `SE = sqrt((Σw² /K − N̂²)/K)`.

**Validation is not optional and I ran it:** on 8×8 [4,3,3,2] where the truth is exactly 3 562 232, SIS gave **3 563 541** at K=200 000 (error **+0.04%**, quoted RSE 0.21% — well inside one sigma) in 965 ms, and 3 554 400 at K=20 000 (error −0.22%, RSE 0.68%) in 130 ms. Dead-end fraction 9.0%. That comparison must exist as a unit test in the shipped project: *the estimator is checked against a number the game can compute exactly*. That is precisely the nostromo-gambit oracle doctrine (self-play with invariants on every ply) applied to a counter.

Dead-end fractions rise with fleet density — 3.6% for 10×10 [4,3,3,2], 5.4% for [5,4,3,3,2], **68.6%** for the Russian fleet. High dead-end fraction is the warning light for variance; if it exceeds ~85%, add look-ahead pruning (reject a candidate if any *later* ship provably has no placement) before increasing K, since pruning cuts variance while K only cuts it as 1/√K.

**Effective sample size.** Track `ESS = (Σw)² / Σw²`. If ESS < 200, the displayed number is not trustworthy at 3 significant digits — round harder (2 sig figs) rather than showing precision you don't have. Widening the displayed precision instead of faking it is the same move as nostromo's «ДОПУСК РАСШИРЕН ДО ±45 СП» written into the log.

## Budget: 60 fps means 16.7 ms of main thread. The oracle gets 0 ms of it.

**Architecture: everything in a Web Worker, built from a Blob URL so the project stays a single self-contained page with zero external assets** (same doctrine as sprites-from-ASCII rather than PNGs). The 13.6 MB array never crosses the worker boundary. Per turn the worker posts back ~**300 bytes**: `{answer, killedShip, before, after, bits, density: Float32Array(64), ghosts: Uint8Array(64), exact}`.

### Measured, 8×8 [4,3,3,2], Node 24, one thread, this laptop

| item | cost |
|---|---|
| build universe (3 562 232 cfgs) | **68 ms** |
| memory, ships array | **13.6 MB** |
| memory, peak total (worker) | ~30 MB RSS |
| turn 1: histogram + partition + compact | **102.6 ms** |
| turn 2 | 71.9 ms |
| turn 5 | 35.0 ms |
| turn 7 | 12.7 ms |
| turn 10 | 4.1 ms |
| turn 13 | 1.1 ms |
| turn 20+ | < 0.1 ms |
| whole 31-turn game, total compute | **360 ms** |
| single partition scan, full universe | 17 ms (bit test) / ~26 ms (table lookup incl. compaction) |
| marginal histogram, full universe | 20.6 ms |

**Worst case is turn 1 at 103 ms, and it is hidden twice over:** the universe build (68 ms) runs behind the boot typewriter (`ВЫЧИСЛИТЕЛЬНЫЙ КОМПЛЕКС · ИНИЦИАЛИЗАЦИЯ`, 9 ms/char × ~140 chars ≈ 1.3 s of cover), and each turn's compute runs behind the shot animation, which should be ≥400 ms anyway for the ghost-fleet reshuffle. The player never waits on the oracle after turn 5.

**Browser vs Node.** Expect V8 in Chrome to be within 10–20% of Node here — it's a flat typed-array scan, no allocation in the hot loop, no GC pressure (the only per-turn allocations are the 290-int bucket array and three 288-byte tables; hoist them into module scope and reuse). Firefox/Safari may be 1.5–2× slower on the byte-gather; budget 200 ms for turn 1 there. Mid-range phone: 3–4× slower ⇒ turn 1 ≈ 350–400 ms, still fully covered by the animation, and 13.6 MB is fine on any phone from the last decade.

**Fallback without a Worker** (if the artifact host blocks Blob workers): time-slice the compaction. Chunks of 300 000 configs cost ~7 ms each; 12 chunks across 12 `requestAnimationFrame` callbacks = 200 ms wall time with no dropped frames. Report progress as a phase-weighted bar exactly like nostromo's drop banner — the four phases write themselves: `СКАН ВЕТВЕЙ…` / `РАЗДЕЛЕНИЕ ИСХОДОВ…` / `СХЛОПЫВАНИЕ…` / `ПЕРЕСЧЁТ`. Note the reference project has no `requestAnimationFrame` anywhere, so this is a genuinely new pattern for the codebase; introduce it deliberately and document it.

**Micro-optimisations that earned their place (all measured, not guessed):**
1. *Per-turn lookup tables (288 bytes) instead of bit tests in the inner loop.* The inner loop becomes 4 byte loads + ≤4 byte lookups, no shifts, no masks.
2. *Marginals over placements, not cells.* 4 increments per config instead of 12, then O(288) expansion. ~3× on the histogram pass.
3. *In-place compaction, no index array.* Sequential access instead of a gathered read through `alive[i]`, and it saves 14 MB. This is worth more than it looks: the gathered variant measured 17 ms/pass on a 27 MB occupancy array; the sequential 4-byte variant does more work per element in comparable time.
4. *Fuse partition and compaction* when the answer policy is pure greedy on a cheap key — or accept two passes (I measured two passes; it's already fast enough, and two passes is clearer code).

**Where it breaks, and the wall.** 8×8 [4,3,3,2,2] is 45 317 068 configs = 226 MB at 5 bytes/config — over the line for a browser tab. **The materialisation ceiling is roughly 10 million configurations (~50 MB).** Anything above it must go to Tier 1 sampling. Concretely: 8×8 with four ships = materialise; 8×8 with five ships, 10×10 with anything, or the no-touch rule disabled (20M for [4,3,3,2]) = borderline-to-sampling. This is exactly why I recommend 8×8 [4,3,3,2] no-touch as the canonical mode and treat 10×10 as an explicitly labelled approximate mode.

**Tier 1 costs, measured.** SIS: 200 000 samples on 8×8 in 965 ms, on 10×10 Russian in 3.0 s ⇒ ~15 µs/sample. A per-turn budget of 20 000 samples = ~300 ms — too slow for every turn on the main thread, fine in a worker, and unnecessary if the population is maintained by Gibbs (a full sweep over 10 ships is ~10 candidate enumerations of ≤180 placements ≈ 2 000 mask tests ≈ 20 µs, so K=1500 particles × 1 sweep ≈ 30 ms). Budget: 30–60 ms/turn in the worker, re-anchor with SIS every 5 turns off the critical path.

**Determinism has no cost.** xorshift128+ (`src/game/rng.mjs`, dropped in unchanged) is ~1 ns/draw and the oracle draws maybe 20 numbers per turn.
data.correctness:
## The defender provably never lies

**Invariant I.** At the start of every turn, `alive` is exactly the set of complete legal fleet placements consistent with the full answer history, and `|alive| ≥ 1`.

**Base case.** `alive₀` = all placements enumerated by `buildUniverse` — legal by construction (no overlap, no touching, no rift cell), consistent with an empty history, and non-empty (3 562 232 > 0; with rifts, assert `> 0` at build time and re-roll the rift seed if a pathological rift set empties it — cannot happen with ≤4 rift cells, but assert anyway).

**Inductive step.** On a shot at cell *c*, `keyOfShot` is a **total function** on `alive`: every configuration maps to exactly one key, because ships never overlap so at most one slot covers *c*, and the kill test `(p.o & ~nshot) === 0` is a decidable predicate on that slot. Therefore the keys **partition** `alive`:  `alive = ⊎_k bucket_k`, and `Σ_k cnt[k] = |alive|`.

`chooseBucket` returns a key with `cnt[chosen] ≥ 1` — for the greedy policy because the argmax of a partition of a non-empty set is non-empty; for the ε-slack policy because the pool is filtered on `cnt[k] > 0`; for the torpedo policy because the min is taken over non-empty buckets only. Hence `alive' = bucket_chosen ≠ ∅`.

Every member of `bucket_chosen` is, by the definition of the key function, a configuration that *would have produced exactly the answer we gave*, and it was already consistent with all prior answers by the inductive hypothesis. So `alive'` is exactly the consistent set for the extended history, and it is non-empty. ∎

**The answer is therefore always backed by an explicit witness**, and not just one: `cnt[chosen]` of them, each materially present in memory as four bytes. At any moment the game can be asked "prove it" and hand back a concrete fleet — a real feature worth shipping («ПОКАЗАТЬ ОДНУ ИЗ РЕАЛЬНОСТЕЙ», draws a sampled config solid).

**The subtle constraint that is handled for free.** The literature-hard part of this problem is the *time-indexed* nature of a hit: "hit, not sunk" at turn *t* asserts that the ship covering *c* had an unshot cell **as of turn t**, and a later shot may legitimately sink it. Any implementation that maintains an explicit constraint set has to carry the shot-set snapshot per answer and re-check it. Here it evaporates: we filtered at turn *t* using `nshot_t`, and the survivors are permanently those that satisfied it. There is no constraint object to get wrong. **This is the single strongest argument for population-as-constraint over solver-as-constraint, and it should be the load-bearing comment at the top of the oracle file.**

**Tier 1 (sampling) needs one extra guarantee**, because there the population is a *sample* of the consistent set, not the set. Maintain `W` — a single witness configuration, always consistent with the full history:
- Each turn, after choosing an answer, set `W := ` any particle in the chosen bucket (there is at least one, or we would not have chosen it).
- If the population is empty or every bucket is empty (sampler failure, not a logical impossibility), **answer as `W` would answer**. `W` is consistent with the whole history by induction, so its answer is legal. The defender degrades from "maximally evasive" to "honest but dumb" — never to "liar".
- Log it: «ОРАКУЛ ОСЛЕП — ОТВЕТ ПО ЯКОРНОЙ ВЕТКЕ». Visible honest degradation, exactly like «ДОПУСК РАСШИРЕН ДО ±45 СП».

## Termination and winnability

**Termination.** Every shot targets a previously unshot cell (the UI must forbid re-shooting, and should, since it yields 0 bits anyway). The potential function `unshotCells` strictly decreases, so the game ends within 64 turns (100 on 10×10). At `unshotCells = 0` every cell's occupancy is determined by the answers, so `|alive| = 1` and every ship is fully within the shot set — meaning every ship was answered KILL at some point. **The player always wins; the only question is in how many shots.** There is no losing state and no draw.

**Under the recommended victory rule (`N == 1`) it terminates much sooner**, and I measured it rather than assuming: 31 turns against an optimal density-guided player (8/8 seeds), 44–52 turns against a parity hunt/target player (mean 48.3), 26–30 with two region probes spent. Information-theoretic floor log₂(3 562 232) = **21.76 bits**, and since a shot has ≥2 outcomes it yields ≤1 bit, so **22 shots is the absolute minimum** and 31 is the realistic par. That gives a clean scoring band: ≤26 «ПРОРОК», 27–31 «НАВИГАТОР», 32–40 «СЛЕПЕЦ».

**Non-degeneracy.** There is no "no valid configuration" state to guard against, because we never construct constraints — we only remove elements from a non-empty set. If `aliveN` ever hits 0, that is not a game state, it is a bug in `compact` or a mismatch between the partition key function and the compaction key function (they must be literally the same function; do not write it twice). `throw new Error('[оракул] множество реальностей опустело')` and let it be loud.

**One more property worth asserting in tests.** The counter must be *consistent with the ghosts*: `density[c] === 0` ⟺ no sampled ghost occupies `c`, and `density[c] === aliveN` ⟺ every ghost occupies it. Cheap invariant, catches key/compaction desync immediately. Alongside: a self-play harness that plays N games with random player policies and asserts on every turn that (a) `aliveN` strictly decreases or stays equal, (b) `aliveN ≥ 1`, (c) a brute-force re-derivation of the consistent set from the raw answer history equals the maintained `alive` set — checkable exactly at 8×8, which is the whole point of choosing 8×8. That is the direct analogue of nostromo's `npm run selfplay` oracle.
data.salvo:
## Everything is one primitive: `partition(keyOf) → chooseBucket(policy) → compact()`

The four weapons differ only in **what the key is** and **which bucket the policy picks**. That is the whole weapon system, and it means new munitions cost ~15 lines each. Worth designing the code around explicitly.

| weapon | key function | policy | cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| ОБЫЧНЫЙ ВЫСТРЕЛ | miss / hit / kill(placementId) | max mass | 1 pass |
| ЗАЛП (m клеток) | tuple of m per-cell answers | max mass | 1 pass |
| ЗОНД (счётная волна) | `popcount(occ ∩ R)` | max mass | 1 pass |
| ПОЛЕ ГЕЛЛЕРА | full occupancy pattern `occ ∩ R` | max mass | 1 pass |
| БРАНА-ТОРПЕДА | miss / hit / kill | **min non-empty** | 1 pass |

### Salvo (simultaneous multi-cell shot)

The answer is a **tuple**, one entry per fired cell, and the population is partitioned by the whole tuple — not cell by cell. Partitioning cell-by-cell and then intersecting would be wrong: it could select a combination of individually-max answers that jointly has zero witnesses, i.e. a lie.

Implementation: build one shot-table triple per fired cell (all against the *post-salvo* shot mask `nshot`, because the salvo lands at once), then one pass over `alive` computing an m-entry signature, densifying signatures into small integer keys via a `Map` filled in traversal order (deterministic). Then the usual argmax + compact. Cost is one pass, m× the per-config work — a 3-cell salvo on turn 1 costs ~150 ms, which is why salvos should be a mid-game munition or the game should simply accept 150 ms in the worker.

**Kill attribution inside a salvo** needs a stated canonical rule, or the same salvo has two legal readings: if two cells of the same salvo complete one ship, the KILL is attributed to the **last cell in raster order** (`r*8+c` ascending) and the earlier one reports HIT. Sort the fired cells before building tables. Write the rule in the log so the player can verify it: «ЗАЛП D4·D5·D6 → МИМО · ПОПАДАНИЕ · УБИТ (3)».

**Why the joint form matters to the player**: a salvo is strictly more informative per shot than the same cells fired sequentially *for the player*, because the defender cannot adapt between them — but it is also strictly *worse*, because the defender picks the best joint answer with full knowledge of all m cells. These two effects are real and opposite; the joint partition is what makes the tradeoff honest. Do not pretend a salvo is just m shots.

### Count probe (счётная волна)

"How many ship cells lie inside region R?" Key = `popcount(occ ∩ R)`, values 0..12. Up to 13 buckets, so the theoretical yield is up to log₂13 = 3.7 bits, but the adversary takes the modal bucket so the practical yield is ~1–1.5 bits — **comparable to a single shot**. I measured this: two 3×3 count probes reduce the optimal game from 31.0 to 28.5 turns, i.e. **≈1.25 turns saved per probe**. So a probe that costs a turn is roughly break-even and therefore boring. Tune it by making the region larger (a full row/column/quadrant), or by making the probe cost a resource rather than a turn.

Note the fleet has 12 cells total, so a probe over the *whole board* always answers 12 and yields 0 bits — a nice teaching moment the UI should refuse politely rather than waste: «ВОЛНА СЛИШКОМ ШИРОКА — ОТВЕТ ИЗВЕСТЕН ЗАРАНЕЕ».

### Geller field (пузырь стабильной реальности) — the strong weapon

This is not a question, it is a **forced commitment**. Key = the full occupancy bit-pattern of `occ ∩ R` (for a 3×3 region, at most 2⁹ = 512 distinct patterns, and in practice far fewer because of the no-touch rule and the fleet's size). The defender must choose one pattern and live with it forever; every cell of R becomes determined in every surviving reality.

This is dramatically stronger than a count probe because it removes *all* internal degrees of freedom in R at once, not just one aggregate number. A 3×3 field typically collapses the counter by an order of magnitude in a single action — it is the cliff-edge moment the counter exists to dramatise, and it is literally «пришпилить реальность» from the seed brainstorm. Balance it as a once-or-twice-per-game resource.

Two follow-on consequences the UI gets for free: pinned cells are permanently painted (all realities agree), and shooting into a pinned region afterwards yields exactly 0.00 bits — which teaches, without a tutorial, that shots must be aimed where the multiverse is *undecided*. That is the whole skill of the game in one visual.

### Brane torpedo (брана-торпеда) — the fun button

Same key function as a normal shot, but `policy = 'torpedo'`: pick the **smallest non-empty** bucket. The god is forced into the answer it least wants, and since HIT/KILL buckets are almost always the minority (the densest cell on turn 1 is occupied in only 22.2% of realities), a torpedo is effectively a **guaranteed hit wherever a hit is possible at all**, plus the largest possible single-shot collapse of the counter. It is still 100% honest — the chosen bucket is non-empty, so a witness exists.

This is the answer to the emotional flatness of a max-mass defender that says MISS 80% of the time. Give the player 2–3 torpedoes per game. In fiction it is exactly the friend's line: «есть особый снаряд которым я могу накрыть сразу несколько альтернативных веток».

### One implementation note that ties them together

`chooseBucket(cnt, policy, eps, rng)` is the *only* place in the entire oracle where a decision is made, and the only place that consumes randomness. Every weapon, every difficulty level, and every replay determinism property funnels through those four arguments. Keep it that way.
data.pitfalls:
## 1. Population collapse to zero
**Tier 0: structurally impossible** — buckets partition a non-empty set and we always pick a non-empty bucket. If it happens, it is a code bug (partition key ≠ compaction key), so *use the same function object for both*, never two copies. Assert `aliveN >= 1` after every compaction and throw loudly.
**Tier 1: possible** (sampler fails to find particles in the true set). Mitigation is the anchor witness `W` described in `correctness`: the defender falls back to answering as one known-consistent configuration would. Also monitor ESS and force a fresh SIS restart when ESS < 200 or when the dead-end fraction of the last batch exceeds 0.9.

## 2. The deterministic-puzzle trap — the biggest design bug, and it is invisible until you measure
With a deterministic greedy defender and *no hidden state*, there is literally nothing hidden: both sides face the same public information set, so the optimal line is identical in every playthrough. My optimal player scored **31, 31, 31, 31, 31, 31, 31, 31** across eight different seeds. The game would have zero replay value and a solved-once-solved-forever optimal opening.
Two fixes, both required:
- **Rift cells** (`riftMask`): 2–4 seeded cells no ship may occupy, folded into the universe build. Different universe, different size, different optimal line every game — and the counter opens on a fresh number each time, which is better theatre than a constant.
- **ε-slack answer selection**: among buckets within `(1−ε)` of the max, choose by seeded weighted RNG. `ε` is the difficulty table, in the nostromo idiom of weakening by choosing among near-optimal moves rather than by crippling the search:
  `1 СЛЕПОЙ ε=0.40 / 2 ШЕПЧУЩИЙ ε=0.22 / 3 ЛОЦМАН ε=0.10 / 4 АРХИВАРИУС ε=0.03 / 5 ТОТ, КТО ЗА БРАНОЙ ε=0` — «Полная жадность. Он не ошибётся ни разу.»

## 3. Sampler bias making the counter lie
**Tier 0 has no sampler**, and this is worth saying in the README as the project's central technical claim. Ghost fleets are `alive[rng.int(0, aliveN-1)]` — exactly uniform over the consistent set, with no weights, no burn-in, no correlation. Density is a full exact count, not a sample.
**Tier 1**: (a) never mix particles produced by different proposals in one estimate — mixing SIS-weighted survivors with fresh Gibbs particles silently biases the ratio; regenerate wholesale or keep the populations separate by role (Gibbs population for decisions and ratios, SIS batches for anchoring only). (b) Gibbs is uniform-stationary but **irreducibility is not guaranteed** on tightly-packed boards — a single-ship move may not connect all configurations. Mitigate with occasional two-ship block moves and periodic independent SIS restarts, and never claim uniformity you haven't tested. (c) *Validate the estimator against a case you can compute exactly* — the 8×8 test (3 563 541 vs 3 562 232, +0.04%) must be a shipped unit test, because it is the only thing standing between "estimator" and "made-up number".

## 4. Floating point
Tier 0 counts are `Int32` up to 3.56M — no float anywhere; use `Int32Array` for buckets, not `Array`. The density array can be `Float64Array` but the values are integers; keep them integral and divide only at render time.
Tier 1: 1.87×10¹⁵ is under 2⁵³ so it is an exact integer in a `Number`, but 1.33×10¹⁸ (touching variant) is **not** — and more importantly a product of ~40 survival ratios drifts and can underflow. **Accumulate the counter in log space** (`logN += Math.log(f)`) and exponentiate only for display. Never compare floats for the monotone clamp; compare the logs.

## 5. RNG determinism and replay
- `Math.random` must appear **zero** times in the oracle. Use `makeRng(seed)` from `src/game/rng.mjs` unchanged, and `fork(label)` per subsystem: `rng.fork('rift')`, `rng.fork('defender')`, `rng.fork('ghosts')`. Without forks, adding one ghost draw shifts every defender decision and old replays break.
- **Map iteration order is a determinism hazard.** Anywhere a bucket set is built from a `Map` (salvos, Geller patterns), the argmax over a `Map` depends on insertion order, which depends on the traversal order of `alive`, which depends on prior compactions. It happens to be deterministic, but it is fragile. Prefer a dense `Int32Array` indexed by key; where a `Map` is unavoidable, **sort the keys before `chooseBucket`** so the RNG consumes draws in a stable order.
- A replay is `{ seed, riftCount, difficulty, shots: [...] }` — nothing else. That is enough to reconstruct the entire game bit-for-bit, which makes bug reports reproducible and makes a «ПОВТОРИТЬ ПАРТИЮ» feature free.

## 6. In-place compaction aliasing
`compact` writes to index `w*4` while reading from `i*4` with `w ≤ i`. When `w === i` the write is a self-overwrite through an alias. Read all four bytes into locals **before** the first store. I hit this while writing the benchmark; it produces a corrupted universe that still looks plausible for several turns — the worst kind of bug. Guard it with the ghost/density consistency assert.

## 7. The one-byte assumption
Placement indices fit in `Uint8Array` only because every list is < 256 (max 180, for length-2 on 10×10). Assert `list.length < 256` at build time and switch the whole array to `Uint16Array` if a future fleet breaks it. Silent truncation here would be catastrophic and invisible.

## 8. The two-clocks problem
Pin at turn 31, last ship sunk at turn 62. Shipping "sink all ships" as the victory condition means half the game is a known-answer mop-up. Victory must be `N == 1`. (Detailed in `approach`.)

## 9. Emotional flatness of a truthful adversary
25 misses / 6 hits / 0 kills along the optimal line. Handled by reframing miss→«РЕАЛЬНОСТЬ СМЕЩАЕТСЯ» with the counter as the payoff, plus the brane torpedo. But be aware it is a real risk: if the ghost fleet and counter are not *immediately* legible, the game reads as "I keep missing" and is abandoned in 90 seconds. The first three shots must teach the loop with no words: big number, big drop, ghosts visibly writhing and thinning.

## 10. Accessibility: flickering ghosts are a genuine hazard
"Faint flickering silhouettes" at high frequency is a photosensitivity risk, not just a taste question. Cap the ghost re-roll at ≤3 Hz, keep contrast low (`--phosphor-faint` on `--dark-square`), and under `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` **stop the flicker entirely** and render a static density heat instead. The reference project has three `prefers-reduced-motion` guards; this project needs a fourth and it is the most important one in either codebase.

## 11. Memory pressure on the wrong platform
13.6 MB is fine; 226 MB (the [4,3,3,2,2] variant) is not. Do not let a "just add one more ship" settings option quietly cross the materialisation ceiling. Gate fleet selection so any fleet whose universe exceeds ~10M configs is explicitly marked as approximate mode in the UI, with the «≈» on the counter — and say so on the start screen the way nostromo says Fischer castling is off.

## 12. Worker availability
Blob-URL workers can be blocked by CSP in some embedding contexts. Detect at boot (`try { new Worker(url) } catch`), and fall back to the `requestAnimationFrame` time-sliced path rather than blocking the main thread for 103 ms. Print the mode in the boot sequence — «ОРАКУЛ · ОТДЕЛЬНЫЙ ПОТОК» vs «ОРАКУЛ · РАЗДЕЛЕНИЕ КАДРОВ» — because an honest status line is cheaper than a mystery stutter.
